account.description: A cloud account's own facts, declared once and shared by every component whose cloud: entry names it.

project.description: The Google Cloud project's ID, as gcloud projects list prints it.

anyOf.description: Google Cloud, where the account is a project named by project:.

provider.description: The cloud the account belongs to.

accountRef.description: One component's use of an account declared under accounts:.

account.description: The name of an entry under accounts:.

regions.description: Regions this component's resources are in. Omit to declare the whole account, which is the only entry that receives the findings belonging to no region, such as the account's IAM policy.

ciConfig.description: What a run records about the CI job it ran in. A run always records who the CI system reports as having started the pipeline and who wrote the commit, as a handle and the platform's stable id; an email address is recorded only when asked for.

recordEmail.description: Also record the email addresses the CI system reports for those two people. Off when absent; when off, no address is read.

cluster.description: A Kubernetes cluster's own facts, declared once and shared by every component whose kubernetes: entry names it.

benchmark.description: The CIS benchmark kube-bench audits this cluster against, such as cis-1.10 or eks-1.5.0. Omit to let kube-bench choose from the cluster's version.

context.description: The kubeconfig context that reaches the cluster. Omit to use the kubeconfig's current context.

anyOf.description: You operate this, so a misconfiguration is yours to change.
A cloud provider operates it, so controls it owns are reported as theirs rather than as yours to fix.

operatedBy.description: Who runs the cluster. "provider" for a managed service, where the control plane, API server and etcd are not reachable by the team that owns the workloads — findings about those are reported but never presented as work this team can do. RBAC, Pod Security and network policy stay theirs either way. Defaults to "self".

version.description: The Kubernetes version kube-bench selects a benchmark from when it cannot read it from the cluster, such as "1.34". Ignored when benchmark is set.

clusterRef.description: One component's use of a cluster declared under clusters:.

cluster.description: The name of an entry under clusters:.

namespaces.description: Namespaces this component owns. Omit to declare the whole cluster, which is the only entry that runs the cluster-wide checks. Only the draugrK8sPolicies scanner can honor a scope; the others refuse rather than silently report the whole cluster.

component.description: One logical part of the app. All surface lists are optional — declare what applies.

anyOf.description: You build this, so a finding in it is yours to fix in the code.
Somebody else publishes this, so the fix is a newer version rather than a change here.

builtBy.description: Who publishes this component's targets, unless one of them says otherwise: "self" (the default) or "upstream". Set it once on a component that is entirely somebody else's software, instead of writing it on every repository and image — where a target added later silently defaults back to self.

trustRoot.description: Path to a Sigstore trusted-root JSON file, for a runner that cannot reach the transparency log. Without one, a runner with no egress reports an error rather than a pass.

history.description: Also scan the repository's commit history, in addition to the working tree. Off by default: it needs a full clone rather than a shallow one, so it is slower on a large repository. A secret committed and later removed is still fetchable by anyone who can clone, so it is still compromised, this is what finds it. History findings are marked as such, because they name the path the secret had when it was introduced, and are kept only when that path would be checked out by this component's paths and ignore. A secret still in the tree at the same path is reported once, as the tree finding.

expiryWarnDays.description: Report a warning when the certificate expires within this many days. Defaults to 30. Lower it for endpoints with automated renewal so the gate only fires when renewal has failed.

criticality.description: Business impact if this component fails — the impact axis of risk prioritization.

dependencyHealthConfig.description: Rank a finding up when the dependency it is in has been deprecated by its publisher or flagged as malicious. Beside `exploitability` and `reachability` because all three decide how findings are ranked. Only statements by somebody who can be named move a finding; health scores are read as context and never change a band, and this never gates on its own.

enabled.description: Turn the signal on. Off when absent. A field rather than the block's presence, because a scan with this on sends the list of packages it found to deps.dev, and writing the block to see what it does should not be the same act as agreeing to that.

excludeRule.description: One exclusion. Set paths, rules, or both; when both are set a finding must match both.

acceptedBy.description: Who decided this finding was acceptable. Optional; a suppression without one is reported as unattributed.

expires.description: Date this exclusion stops applying (YYYY-MM-DD). Past it the finding returns and the report says the exclusion lapsed.

paths.description: Location patterns. A pattern ending in '/' matches everything beneath that directory; otherwise it is a glob against the whole location.

reason.description: Why this exclusion exists. Required: an exclusion without a reason is indistinguishable from an oversight.

rules.description: Rule ids to suppress, matched exactly.

exploitabilityConfig.description: Severity enrichment from real-world exploitability signals: CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog and FIRST's EPSS scores. A CVE on KEV becomes critical; a CVE at or above the EPSS threshold is raised one band. Applied before ranking, so priority reflects what is being exploited rather than only what could be. Either signal works without the other. Fetch the data with `draugr feeds update`.

epss.description: Where the EPSS scores come from: a file path, "cache", or "auto" — the same three choices as kev. Omit to leave EPSS off.

epssThreshold.description: EPSS probability at or above which a finding's severity is raised one band. Defaults to 0.5 — a coin-flip chance of exploitation within 30 days. Scores are heavily skewed, so lowering this widens the net faster than the number suggests. Zero disables the EPSS bump while leaving KEV in force.

kev.description: Where the KEV catalog comes from: a file path, "cache" to read ~/.draugr/feeds without touching the network, or "auto" to fetch when the cache is missing or stale. Omit to leave KEV off.

maxAge.description: How old a cached feed may be before "auto" refetches it and a scan warns that it is stale. It is also the age at which govulncheck stops reading the local Go vulnerability database. A Go duration; defaults to 24h, tracking EPSS being republished daily. Raise it on a runner deliberately pinned to a known copy of the data.

Any rated finding fails the build.
The SARIF level a gate used to take; the same as high.
The SARIF level a gate used to take; the same as medium.
The SARIF level a gate used to take; the same as low.

failOn.description: What fails the build, in either vocabulary. A priority band (P1-P4) asks what band a finding landed in for the component it was found in, folding in the exposure and criticality declared below. A severity (critical, high, medium, low) asks what the scanner called the flaw on its own terms. Empty is the default, which is P1.

failOnCaveats.description: Kinds of caveat that fail the run as an error does: reported with the errors, the component reads ERROR, and --allow-scan-errors accepts it. Empty fails on none.

anyOf.description: A surface a component declares that no enabled control looks at.
A scanner that cannot honor a component's scope, so it did not run for that component.
A dependency file or Terraform module, in a repository that was read, that no scanner read.
A cloud check the scan could not evaluate, because a read it needs was denied.
An imported SARIF file that states no revision, so nothing shows it describes the code being scanned.

failOnPriority.description: Deprecated: write the band in failOn, which takes either vocabulary. Still read, so a descriptor that predates the merge keeps working, and refused alongside failOn.

anyOf.description: Served to browsers — full security-header suite (default).
API endpoint — skips browser-only headers.

url.description: Endpoint URL. Must be https:// for the tls control.

hostAuth.description: Authenticate the dynamic scan of this endpoint. Absent means probe it anonymously — which, against an application that requires a login, tests the login page and reports a pass about everything behind it.

header.description: Header name, required with type "header" (e.g. X-API-Key).

tokenEnv.description: Environment variable holding the credential. There is deliberately no field for the credential itself: a descriptor is committed, so a token written into one is a leaked token.

anyOf.description: Sends Authorization: Bearer <token>.
Sends a header you name — e.g. X-API-Key.

hostSpec.description: Drive the dynamic scan from an OpenAPI document instead of crawling. An API usually has no HTML to crawl, so a specification is what turns guessing into exercising the routes the service declares.

methods.description: HTTP methods to exercise. Absent means GET and HEAD. Naming a write method is how you accept that the scan may change data — a specification lists DELETE too, and a scanner handed one will use it.

path.description: The OpenAPI or Swagger document, relative to the descriptor.

anyOf.description: You build this, so a finding in it is yours to fix in the code.
Somebody else publishes this, so the fix is a newer version rather than a change here.

builtBy.description: Who builds this image: "self" (the default) or "upstream" for one this component runs but somebody else publishes. It decides what the report tells you to do about a vulnerable package inside it — a library in an image you build is yours to upgrade, and the same library in an image you only run is fixed by taking a newer image.

digest.description: Pin the immutable content digest, e.g. sha256:…

signedBy.description: The signer this image is expected to carry, from config.controls.provenance.signers, whatever that signer's own image patterns say. For the one image that came from somewhere else; a signer states which images it covers, so a project whose registry is its own needs nothing here.

import.description: A SARIF file another tool wrote about this component, read into one of Draugr's controls.

control.description: The control the file's findings belong to, such as sast or sca.

file.description: The SARIF 2.1.0 file, relative to where Draugr runs.

issueItem.description: Metadata set on an issue or work item when it is created. A later run adds back a configured label or tag that was removed and changes nothing else.

areaPath.description: azure-work-item: the area path, such as Shop\Payments. Defaults to the project's default area.

assignedTo.description: azure-work-item: the identity a new work item is assigned to, as an email address or display name.

assignees.description: github-issue, gitlab-issue: logins on GitHub, usernames on GitLab.

confidential.description: gitlab-issue: whether a new issue is visible only to project members. Defaults to true.

fields.description: azure-work-item: other fields set on a new work item, by reference name, such as Microsoft.VSTS.Common.Severity.

iterationPath.description: azure-work-item: the iteration path, such as Shop\Sprint 12. Defaults to the project's default iteration.

labels.description: github-issue, gitlab-issue: labels applied beside the tracking label.

milestone.description: github-issue, gitlab-issue: a milestone's title, open or closed.

tags.description: azure-work-item: tags applied beside the tracking tag.

type.description: An issue type the organization defines on GitHub; issue, incident or task on GitLab; a work item type on Azure DevOps, defaulting to the default type of the Task category.

anyOf.description: GitLab's default issue type.
A service disruption, listed under the project's incidents. Needs the Reporter role.
A planning item that sits under an issue.

branches.description: github-issue, gitlab-issue, azure-work-item: the branches whose runs open, rewrite and close issues, as names or globs. Defaults to the repository's default branch.

anyOf.description: One issue listing every action.
A parent issue with a child per action.
A parent issue with a child per control.

children.description: github-issue, gitlab-issue, azure-work-item: one issue, or a parent with a child per action or per control. Defaults to none.

item.description: github-issue, gitlab-issue, azure-work-item: the metadata set on an issue or work item when it is created.

anyOf.description: Write each report into a directory.
Upload the SARIF report to GitHub code scanning.
Post the Markdown report as a sticky pull-request comment.
Keep a GitHub issue open while the gate fails, and close it when the gate passes.
Post the Markdown report as a sticky Azure DevOps pull-request comment.
Keep an Azure Boards work item open while the gate fails, and close it when the gate passes.
Post the Markdown report as a sticky GitLab merge-request comment.
Keep a GitLab issue open while the gate fails, and close it when the gate passes.
Post the run to any server implementing Draugr's run-ingest API, such as Draugr Cloud. Requires the json and sarif report formats.

label.description: github-issue, gitlab-issue, azure-work-item: the label, or tag on Azure DevOps, that finds this entry's items, applied to each one. Defaults to draugr.

labelBy.description: github-issue, gitlab-issue, azure-work-item: the facts every run keeps on an issue as labels, adding the ones that apply and removing the ones that no longer do. Defaults to priority. [] keeps none.

anyOf.description: draugr:priority:P1, the highest band among the findings the issue lists.
draugr:control:sca, for each control with a finding the issue lists.
draugr:exposure:public, for each exposure among the components with a finding the issue lists.
draugr:criticality:critical, for each criticality among the components with a finding the issue lists.
draugr:incomplete, while a scan error stops a control the issue covers.

marker.description: github-pr-comment / azure-pr-comment / gitlab-mr-comment: hidden marker identifying the sticky comment to update.

maxChildren.description: github-issue, gitlab-issue, azure-work-item: the most children each parent has open, with children: actions or controls. Defaults to 100.

anyOf.description: Blocks a release: urgent in this component's context.
Scheduled work.
Backlog.
Noted, rarely acted on.

minPriority.description: github-issue, gitlab-issue, azure-work-item: the lowest band that opens an issue. The body lists only the actions at or above it. Defaults to every band.

org.description: azure-pr-comment, azure-work-item: collection URI. Defaults to $SYSTEM_TEAMFOUNDATIONCOLLECTIONURI.

pr.description: github-pr-comment / azure-pr-comment: pull-request number; gitlab-mr-comment: merge-request IID. Defaults to the CI environment.

project.description: azure-pr-comment, azure-work-item: team project. Defaults to $SYSTEM_TEAMPROJECT.

repo.description: github: owner/name (default $GITHUB_REPOSITORY). azure-pr-comment: repository name (default $BUILD_REPOSITORY_NAME). gitlab-mr-comment: project id or full path (default $CI_PROJECT_ID).

reports.description: What this destination delivers. A publisher that can deliver only one format renders it for itself and needs none; `file` has no format of its own, so it needs these.

select.description: github-issue, gitlab-issue, azure-work-item: the part of the run this entry's issues cover. Defaults to the whole run.

anyOf.description: One issue for everything the entry covers.
One issue per control.
One issue per component.

split.description: github-issue, gitlab-issue, azure-work-item: one issue, or one per control or component. Defaults to none.

tokenEnv.description: Environment variable holding the token (default GITHUB_TOKEN; SYSTEM_ACCESSTOKEN for azure-pr-comment and azure-work-item; GITLAB_TOKEN for gitlab-mr-comment). The token itself is never stored in the Saga.

url.description: draugr-api: where the server is reached. Defaults to $DRAUGR_API_URL. The token comes from $DRAUGR_API_TOKEN (or tokenEnv) and never from this file.

publisherSelect.description: The part of a run an issue entry covers, with the meaning of --components, --labels and --controls. A list matches any of its values, every label must match, and the keys together narrow.

labels.description: Component labels, each of which must match.

reachabilityConfig.description: Rank a dependency finding down when this project's code cannot reach the vulnerable part of it. Beside `exploitability` because both decide how findings are ranked, in opposite directions, and both can move a finding across the gate.

analyzers.description: Tools that decide reachability, e.g. `govulncheck`. Named rather than inferred, so the descriptor says which tool reached the verdict and `draugr doctor` can say what to install. An analyzer adds no findings: it ranks findings you already have downward.

release.description: Identifies what is being assessed. Optional; its version labels the reports.

version.description: Release version, shown on every report and appended to the VEX product identifier. Supports ${{ ENV_VAR }} substitution.

filename.description: Override the artifact's default output filename.

anyOf.description: The terminal report, for a run somebody is watching.
The console report plus what makes it defensible: tools, revisions, and what each control measured against.
GitLab Code Quality: every finding, in the merge request, on any tier.
The same, for vulnerable packages in a container image.
The SBOM as GitLab reads it, filling the Dependency List and License Compliance.
The same, for vulnerable dependencies.
GitLab's own security schema, for its Vulnerability Report. A build artifact rather than an upload.
The same, for leaked credentials.
A self-contained page, for attaching to a ticket or an audit.
The whole run as one document, for a platform or a script.
One failed test per finding, for a CI test panel.
The report as prose and tables, for a merge request comment or a wiki.
SARIF 2.1.0, which code scanning and editors read.
Your own layout, from --template or --template-file.
An OpenVEX document saying which vulnerabilities apply to this product.

minPriority.description: Narrow this report to findings at or above a priority band, leaving every other report complete. The artifact states the band it was narrowed to.

template.description: Inline Go text/template (format: template). Set exactly one of template / templateFile.

templateFile.description: Path to a Go text/template (format: template).

anyOf.description: You build this, so a finding in it is yours to fix in the code.
Somebody else publishes this, so the fix is a newer version rather than a change here.

builtBy.description: Who publishes this repository: "self" (the default) or "upstream" for one this component uses and somebody else maintains. Falls back to the component's own builtBy. It decides what the report tells you to do — a denied license in the dependency tree of a repository you do not publish is not one you chose and not one you can swap out, so "change the code" is the wrong advice.

ignore.description: Remove matching paths from the scan, applied after `paths`. Gitignore-style: a trailing `/` is a directory, `*` matches within a path segment, `**` across them.

paths.description: Restrict the scan to these directories and files. A root file is scanned only when an entry names it; the scanners' configuration at the root (.trivyignore, .semgrepignore, .gitleaks.toml and similar) is always kept. An entry the repository does not hold is an error.

revision.description: Branch, tag, or commit to scan.

url.description: Repository URL, or a local path such as `.`

sbomConfig.description: Software Bill of Materials generation. Evidence rather than a control: an SBOM is an inventory of what a component contains, so it finds nothing and never affects the verdict. One document is produced per distinct repository and image. Requires the syft tool.

enabled.description: Generate an SBOM for every repository and image in the project.

anyOf.description: CycloneDX as JSON. The widest support among scanners and platforms, and what GitLab reads.
CycloneDX as XML, for a consumer that asks for it specifically.
SPDX as JSON. Common where licensing and compliance tooling is the consumer.
SPDX in its own tag-value text format, the oldest of the four.

format.description: SBOM document format. Defaults to cyclonedx-json. CycloneDX and SPDX are each offered in both of their standard encodings; pick whichever your consumer reads.

anyOf.description: One document per component, describing what that part of the application ships.
One document for the whole project, describing what the release ships.
A document per component and one for the project.

scope.description: What each document covers. component (default) is one per repository and image; project is one covering the whole release, assembled along the hierarchy the Saga declares; both emits the parts and the whole. project and both require format cyclonedx-json.

vexConfig.description: Who is making the claims in a generated VEX document, and what product they are about. Both optional and both worth setting for a document you publish.

author.description: Who is making these statements — an organization, ideally with a contact. Defaults to the release name, which is a project rather than a party.

product.description: The product the statements are about, as an IRI; a package URL is conventional. Defaults to a purl over the release. Set it to whatever the SBOM your consumer holds calls this product, or nothing will match.

vexDecision.description: What this suppression claims in VEX terms, for `--report vex`. Optional: without it the finding is reported as affected, the reading that is never an overstatement.

anyOf.description: The component is not included in the product at all.
The component is included, but the vulnerable code is not, typically because of how it was configured or built.
The vulnerable code is present and cannot be executed as the product uses it: the product does not call it.
The vulnerable code does run, and nothing an attacker supplies reaches it. The specification calls this difficult to prove conclusively.
Built-in protections completely prevent exploitation by known attack vectors, and a user cannot disable them.

justification.description: Why the product is not affected, from VEX's fixed vocabulary. Valid only with status not_affected; without it the exclusion's reason is emitted as prose.

anyOf.description: No remediation is required regarding this vulnerability. Requires a justification.
Actions are recommended to remediate or address this vulnerability.
These product versions contain a fix for the vulnerability.

status.description: The claim. under_investigation is not accepted here: it is what an untriaged finding already reports, and a finding you have suppressed is one you have finished investigating.

vexRepository.description: A VEX document inside a git repository, for a supplier who publishes there rather than at a stable URL. Cloned with whatever credentials git already has on the machine, so a private repository works and no token belongs here.

path.description: The document's path inside the repository.

ref.description: The branch, tag or commit to read. Empty takes the default branch. Worth pinning for a claim you gate on; either way the report records the commit actually read.

vexSource.description: Where one supplier's VEX document comes from. Exactly one of path, url or repository — naming a source is how you accept its claims, and the report names their author on every finding they excused.

path.description: A document on disk, resolved relative to where Draugr runs — not to the descriptor and not to the repository, which is the rule every other path in a descriptor follows.

url.description: A document to fetch over HTTPS. Fetched once per run and cached; the report records the URL, when it was fetched and the digest of what came back.

description: The draugr.saga.yaml descriptor — a declarative account of an application's security surface and the controls that must pass. See https://draugr.dev/docs/latest/reference/saga-schema/

accounts.description: The cloud accounts the components run in, each declared once by a name that components' cloud: entries refer to.

clusters.description: The Kubernetes clusters the components run on, each declared once by a name that components' kubernetes: entries refer to.

components.description: The app's parts. Each component declares the surfaces it exposes; Draugr plans scans per surface.

fragments.description: Saga fragments to merge into this descriptor.

project.description: Which project this descriptor describes: lowercase letters, digits and dashes. A platform files runs under it.

references.description: Links to manual or human-performed controls (threat model, architecture diagram, …).

title: Draugr Saga
